4.23 Rio Grande. Hydroelectric releases of the magnitude of 4,000 cfs from Amistad Reservoir will result in a very rapid increase in downstream flows, but they will be completely confined within the Rio Grande channel. Fluctuations in downstream flow levels will occur from the hydroelectric releases. These fluctuations will be greatest immediately below Amistad Dam and will decrease with distance downstream. Although the river fluctuation depends on many variables, the river is predicted to rise about 4 feet in the reach from Amistad Dam to the Maverick Canal. In the reach from Maverick Canal to Eagle Pass the Rio Grande will rise less than 3 feet. Below Eagle Pass the river should not fluctuate more than 2 feet.
4.24 Air Quality. The operation of a hydropower facility at Amistad Dam should not have a significant impact upon air quality. With the exception of perhaps several diesel engines used for emergency power generation or for operating compressors, there should not be significant emissions produced from the hydropower facility.
4.25 Amistad Reservoir Water Quality. Past studies indicate that hypolimnion discharges tend to hinder stratification thereby increasing depths which contain adequate dissolved oxygen, normal lake temperature, etc., (Martin and Stroud, 1973). The extent to which the addition of hydropower facilities at Amistad Reservoir will reduce stratification is not known. However, any decrease in the degree of stratification of the reservoir could probably be viewed as beneficial as it would increase the volume for maintaining aquatic life. In addition, with significant destratification occurring, downstream adverse effects could be reduced.
4.26 Rio Grande Water Quality. Hydropower releases will be made through penstocks which will withdraw water from near the reservoir bottom. Based on the available data, the critical period during which time the water quality is likely to be significantly degraded as a result of hydropower releases will occur after the month of May until sometime in late November to early December. Releases made from this bottom layer with near zero or zero oxygen levels can cause a slight increase in ammonia and sulfides, as well as lower dissolved oxygen and temperature downstream. The probable extent of water quality degradation in downstream reaches of the Rio Grande as a result of hydropower releases from Amistad Reservoir cannot be accurately determined with the available data. A short field survey was conducted in April 1976 during which time releases were made through the penstocks. However, the present structure through which these low level releases were made provides for significant reaeration, a situation that will not exist during hydropower releases. Based on observations, the flow measuring weirs located 2.2 miles below the dam and 12.6 miles downstream at Del Rio, should provide significant aeration to maintain oxygen at levels to support aquatic life during the critical release period below these structures. Water quality with respect to aquatic life may be unacceptable in the first 2.2 miles below the dam during critical releases, i.e., releases after May until late November or early December. The primary impact will result from the released water being 10 to 12 degrees colder (centigrade scale) and containing low or negligible oxygen.
4.27 Sanitation. The operation of hydropower facilities at Amistad Dam should not create a significant problem in the area of sanitation. Existing facilities for solid waste disposal and handling wastewater are sufficient for present and future personnel. No problem in the area of sanitation or resulting impacts is envisioned.
